svg.aria-label: Diagram: the three kinds of Google Cloud service account, the five ways a service account is not a user account, the unique ID that role bindings actually use rather than the email address, and the automatic Editor grant on default service accounts
svg.title: Service accounts: three kinds, five ways they are not user accounts, and one automatic grant
svg.text: It has an email address and sits beside people in the policy. It is still not a user account.
The word “account” implies something created on purpose, belonging to someone, listed in a directory. None hold reliably.
User-managed
You create it, in a project you pick.
Yours to update, disable, delete —
and to decide who may act as it.
The only kind anybody chose.
Default
Appears when you enable a service.
NOT Google-managed — it is a
user-managed account you did not ask for.
Your problem, nobody chose its permissions.
Service agents
Google creates them to act for a service.
Each is tied to a resource, which
defines the scope it acts on.
Hold roles on your project — and are
HIDDEN from the IAM page by default.
Five ways it is not a user account
1. Not in your domain — sharing a Workspace asset with everyone does not reach it.
2. Cannot move — the project you create it in is permanent, so centralising is a real decision.
3. Its address is not its identity — bindings use a unique ID; the email is a label on top.
4. It is also a RESOURCE (#31) — who may act as it is a separate policy from what it can do.
5. Dormant after 180 days is a report, not a revocation. Nothing stops working.
Delete, and the grant outlives the account
Role bindings are NOT immediately deleted — the principal is rewritten with the deleted: prefix (#33).
So an audit reads grants that apply to nobody, and a rebuild by the same name comes back with
no permissions and no attachment to its instance.
Disable first. A disabled account can be re-enabled, and tells you what still depended on it.
The catch, taken apart with the posts before it
A default service account may be granted EDITOR on the project, automatically.
#32 — Editor is a LEGACY basic role: it confers permissions not listed in it, so you cannot audit it
by reading the role.
#37 — legacy basic roles cannot carry a condition, so it cannot be time-boxed or scoped.
Unauditable role + no condition + an account nobody created + the whole project.
Fix: enforce iam.automaticIamGrantsForDefaultServiceAccounts (#22).
The date is the part to check, not assume
Enforced by default only for organizations created AFTER 3 May 2024. Older ones: somebody had to turn it on.
Nobody decided to give a project-wide legacy basic role to a machine identity. A service was enabled, and a grant came with it.
